section_summary: This section begins with telegrams and cross-reference sheets documenting the orderly May–June 1932 withdrawal of Japanese forces from Shanghai-area positions and the restoration of Chinese police control. It then contains extensive diplomatic and military intelligence on Japanese troop strength and deployments in Manchuria, Korea, North China, and Jehol, including assessments of Japanese-Soviet tensions and detailed divisional dispositions. Later documents trace renewed movements toward northern frontiers in 1933–1936 and large-scale embarkations and deployments associated with the Sino-Japanese War in 1938.

subfiles.title: Telegram 251 on Japanese withdrawals from Jiangwan, Zhenru, and Zhabei
subfiles.about: Reports witnessed and scheduled Japanese withdrawals from positions in the Shanghai area.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Soule witnessed a Japanese infantry battalion leave Jiangwan and saw one hundred Peiping police resume control without incident. The Japanese military attaché stated that the Zhenru defense unit and the naval landing party in Zhabei would withdraw on May 23.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for withdrawal from Yanghang
subfiles.about: Indexes a report concerning the proposed Japanese withdrawal from Yanghang.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references file 894.23/71 to another decimal-file entry. Its annotation says the Japanese commissioner notified the Chinese commissioner of a plan to withdraw troops from Yanghang.

subfiles.title: Telegram 255 on planned withdrawal from Yanghang and Szetseling
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese plans to leave Yanghang and Szetseling on May 24.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese commissioner notified his Chinese counterpart that the army intended to withdraw from Yanghang and Szetseling at 11 a.m. on May 24. Cunningham repeated the message to the American Legation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for the May 25 Japanese withdrawal
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram concerning arrangements for the withdrawal of Japanese troops.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Cunningham's telegram 256 and a related decimal-file item. It notes that the Chinese police corps had been instructed to make the necessary arrangements for the withdrawal.

subfiles.title: Telegram 256 on withdrawal from Baoshan and Wusong
subfiles.about: Transmits the Japanese commissioner's notice of troop withdrawals scheduled for May 25.
subfiles.summary: Japanese troops were to leave the walled city of Baoshan, the Wusong forts and military facilities, and the portion of Wusong east of the railway. Chinese special police were asked to arrange the transfer, while Japan reserved continued use of temporary billeting localities authorized by the May 5 agreement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for withdrawal near Yanghang
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on the completed Japanese withdrawal from Yanghang and the return of Chinese police.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to telegram 261 and a related file entry. It records that Lieutenant Soule witnessed both the withdrawal and the resumption of control by Chinese special police.

subfiles.title: Telegram 261 on restoration of Chinese control near Yanghang
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese evacuation of Yanghang and Szetseling and discusses an additional transfer of territory.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Soule witnessed the Japanese defense force withdraw and Chinese special police resume control without incident. Colonel Harata offered to transfer another area east of the Shanghai–Wusong Railway, except for the tract extending to Hongkou Creek, once the Chinese declared themselves ready.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for withdrawal from Baoshan
subfiles.about: Indexes the witnessed Japanese withdrawal from Baoshan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references telegram 266 and another decimal-file entry. It notes that Lieutenant Soule saw Chinese special police resume control after the Japanese withdrawal.

subfiles.title: Telegram 266 on evacuation of Baoshan and Wusong
subfiles.about: Reports the withdrawal of the Japanese 6th Brigade and restoration of Chinese control.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Soule witnessed the 6th Brigade leave Baoshan, the Wusong forts, and Wusong east of the railway, after which Chinese special police took control without incident. Colonel Harata said the last Japanese army units would embark for Japan early in June and that three temporary station areas would then revert to China.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for lifting Shanghai's state of emergency
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram linking the end of the emergency to Japanese withdrawal from Hongkou.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the state of emergency would end on June 30. It adds that this was expected to facilitate the departure of Japanese troops from Hongkou under the May 5 agreement.

subfiles.title: Telegram 288 on withdrawal of Shanghai's state of emergency
subfiles.about: Reports the decision to terminate Shanghai's state of emergency on June 30.
subfiles.summary: Cunningham states that the state of emergency would be withdrawn on the morning of June 30. In his view, the change would facilitate the departure of Japanese troops from Hongkou under the agreement of May 5, 1932.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Amano Brigade movement to Nehe
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that part of Amano's brigade entered Nehe.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to telegram 663 and a Manchuria file. It records a Japanese military report that troops from Qiqihar entered Nehe on June 14.

subfiles.title: Telegram 663 on fighting near Keshan
subfiles.about: Forwards Harbin information on a Japanese advance from Qiqihar and fighting near Keshan.
subfiles.summary: Japanese military sources said that part of Amano's brigade entered Nehe on June 14. Press reports added that the same forces defeated approximately six hundred rebel troops seven miles from Keshan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Harbin troop-concentration despatch
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch on Japanese troop concentrations around Harbin.
subfiles.summary: The sheet links file 894.23/77 to despatch 5428 and a Manchuria file. Its subject annotation says Japanese forces around Harbin substantially exceeded peacetime requirements.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese troop concentration and military policy in Manchuria
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese troop concentrations, operations, and military-political calculations in northern Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Despite severe OCR damage, the despatch describes Japanese forces assembling around Harbin and along strategic railway and frontier regions in numbers greater than normal peacetime needs. It discusses operations around the Songhua River and Yilan, the reinforcement of field forces, and the consolidation of occupied territory before further action. The report also links these deployments to Japanese concerns about the Soviet Union and to the influence of the military faction inside Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Japanese troop dispositions in Manchuria
subfiles.about: Indexes a memorandum showing the disposition of Japanese troops in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to a related Manchuria file. It identifies the underlying item as a memorandum from Mukden on Japanese troop locations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Japanese troops at Qiqihar
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch estimating General Amano's force at Qiqihar.
subfiles.summary: The sheet links file 894.23/79 to despatch 5424 and a Manchuria file. It summarizes the report as placing approximately five thousand Japanese troops under General Amano at Qiqihar.

subfiles.title: Despatch 5424 on General Amano's force at Qiqihar
subfiles.about: Reports the composition, financing, and political setting of the Japanese force based at Qiqihar.
subfiles.summary: The despatch and its enclosure describe General Amano's brigade, its artillery, engineers, tanks, motor vehicles, aircraft, trains, and medical equipment. They state that the force protected the Qiqihar region and railway while Japanese troops concentrated farther east, and they discuss the substantial expense of maintaining it. The report also considers Japanese military-faction personalities and relations with Chinese figures including General Ma, Tang Yulin, and Wan Fulin.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for report on the Shanghai withdrawal
subfiles.about: Indexes a report concerning the withdrawal of Japanese troops from Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The sheet links file 894.23/80 to another political-reporting file. Its sole subject is the Japanese withdrawal from Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for transfer of the Hongkou district
subfiles.about: Indexes the return to Chinese control of territory east of the Shanghai–Wusong Railway.
subfiles.summary: The damaged sheet notes that a Hongkou-area tract was transferred to Chinese control. Extra Settlement Roads were excepted, and Japanese forces were described as confined to their remaining positions.

subfiles.title: Telegram 297 on evacuation of eastern Hongkou
subfiles.about: Reports the transfer of eastern Hongkou to Chinese control and lists remaining Japanese positions.
subfiles.summary: The district east of the Shanghai–Wusong Railway returned to Chinese control, except for Extra Settlement Roads. The Japanese naval landing party said it had generally resumed its pre-January 28 positions, with exceptions including several mills, Tungwen College, and Area D. Lieutenant Boone and other neutral observers witnessed the evacuation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Japanese reinforcements arriving at Dalian
subfiles.about: Indexes reports that Japanese reinforcements landing at Dalian might proceed to the Siberian border.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to telegram 671 and a Manchuria file. It records unconfirmed information that reinforcements arriving June 14–15 were destined for the Soviet frontier.

subfiles.title: Telegram 671 on Japanese reinforcements at Dalian
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, Peiping, forwarding the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports the arrival and composition of major Japanese reinforcements at Dalian.
subfiles.summary: Confidential information placed more than ten thousand men and three thousand horses aboard troopships arriving at Dalian on June 14–15, with more ships expected. The force reportedly included cavalry, artillery, machine-gun, telegraph, aviation, motor, and medical units. Unconfirmed reports assigned the troops to the Siberian border.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Japanese relief troops bound for Tianjin
subfiles.about: Indexes a Japanese plan to send troops to Tianjin to relieve units stationed there.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to telegram 164 and a Manchuria file. Its annotation records a planned rotation or reinforcement of the Japanese garrison at Tianjin.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for memoranda on Japanese troops in North Manchuria
subfiles.about: Indexes despatch 5457 and its memoranda on Japanese troop locations.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a related Manchuria file. It identifies the attached materials as memoranda concerning the location of Japanese forces in North Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Despatch and memoranda on the military situation in North Manchuria
subfiles.about: Provides detailed intelligence on Japanese, Soviet, and Chinese forces in northern Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Hanson forwards confidential findings on the locations, mobilization, supplies, and strength of Japanese troops, together with estimates of Soviet and Chinese forces. A translated table lists Japanese divisions and brigades across Manchuria, North China, and railway corridors. The accompanying analysis portrays Japanese expansion as directed toward mainland hegemony and an eventual confrontation with both the Soviet Union and the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for estimate of Japanese forces in Manchuria
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch enclosing an ex-army officer's estimate of Japanese troop strength.
subfiles.summary: The sheet links file 894.23/85 to despatch 5467 and a Manchuria file. It says Hanson forwarded despatch 2361 to the Legation at Peiping with an estimate of Japanese troops compiled by a former army officer.

subfiles.title: Despatch 5467 forwarding an estimate of Japanese troops in Manchuria
subfiles.about: Forwards a numerical estimate of Japanese military forces deployed in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Hanson transmits a copy of an earlier communication to the Legation at Peiping concerning the number of Japanese troops in Manchuria. The enclosure, badly degraded in OCR, tabulates divisions and other formations and attempts to reach a total strength estimate.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for estimate of Japanese troops on the Asian mainland
subfiles.about: Indexes the military attaché's estimate of Japanese troops on the Asian mainland.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to telegram 35 and another file entry. Its subject annotation identifies the underlying information as the military attaché's troop estimate.

subfiles.title: Telegram 35 on Japanese troop strength in Asia
subfiles.about: Transmits the military attaché's estimate of Japanese forces in Manchuria, Korea, North China, and Rehe.
subfiles.summary: The attaché estimated that Japan would have at least ninety-two thousand regular troops on the Asian mainland by February 15, including seventy thousand in Manchuria. At least twenty-one thousand troops were considered available for Rehe operations, with the capacity to double that force by March 1. Available information did not indicate an immediate movement into Rehe in force.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Japanese troop movements through Tianjin
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on ten days of Japanese troop movements through Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to a Tianjin telegram and a related file. Its subject is the recent passage of Japanese troops and supply traffic through the city.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese military traffic through Tianjin and Shanhaiguan
subfiles.about: Reports eastbound military trains and the Japanese disposition at Shanhaiguan.
subfiles.summary: Troop and supply trains had averaged about two per day through Tianjin for ten days. General Suzuki had moved his headquarters from Shanhaiguan to Jinzhou, leaving one regiment, one tank, and two armored trains at Shanhaiguan. Conditions around Qinhuangdao and Shanhaiguan were otherwise described as substantially unchanged.

subfiles.title: Translation of a Chinese Foreign Ministry cable on mobilization through Korea
subfiles.about: Reports the scale of a Japanese troop mobilization routed through Korea.
subfiles.summary: Reliable sources reportedly said mobilization through Korea was completed on February 6. Twenty-four trains carried about thirty thousand infantry, cavalry, and artillery personnel, together with ammunition, provisions, horses, armored cars, guns, and machine guns.

subfiles.title: State Department abstract of the January 24 military attaché report
subfiles.about: Summarizes a military attaché report on Japanese preparations in Manchuria and Rehe.
subfiles.summary: The abstract covers troop movements, the possible creation of a Mongolian army, a planned Manchukuo tour by specialists and journalists, and reservist colonization. It emphasizes that newly called conscripts would train in Manchuria, temporarily raising Japan's active force there to at least seventy thousand.

subfiles.title: Military attaché report on Manchuria, Rehe, and Japanese Army developments
subfiles.doc_type: military intelligence report with routing sheet
subfiles.from: A. W. Brown, Assistant Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. War Department and listed recipients
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese and Manchukuo preparations for possible operations in Rehe and reports related army developments.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the immediate dispatch of new conscripts to Manchuria and assesses the possible timing of a Rehe offensive. It reviews plans for Manchukuo and Mongolian forces, the return of the Japanese 2nd Division, military communications and colonization projects, and planned mechanized and cavalry maneuvers. Supplementary notes record continuing troop movements and argue that Japan might retain older conscript classes until the Rehe question was settled.

subfiles.title: State Department abstract of the February 7 troop-strength report
subfiles.about: Summarizes the military attaché's estimate of Japanese troop strength on the Asian mainland.
subfiles.summary: The abstract gives a February 15 estimate of at least ninety-three thousand troops, including twenty-nine thousand still en route. It notes that returning older conscripts could reduce the total to approximately seventy-one thousand, although army troops might replace part of that reduction. Some sources expected a permanent Manchurian garrison of sixty-five thousand.

subfiles.title: Military attaché estimate and distribution of Japanese forces
subfiles.about: Tabulates Japanese units on the Asian mainland and calculates projected strength after reinforcement and demobilization.
subfiles.summary: The report lists divisions, railway guards, artillery, engineers, transport units, hospitals, aviation, military police, and other formations in Manchuria, Korea, and North China. It estimates a mainland total of roughly ninety-three thousand by February 15, 1933. The author then considers the effect of returning approximately eighteen thousand older conscripts from Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Japanese military activity connected with Russia
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram concerning Japanese military preparations in Manchukuo and the Soviet situation.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to telegram 797 and another file. It characterizes the reported requisitions and movements as probably connected with relations with Russia.

subfiles.title: Telegram 797 on requisitions and northbound equipment in Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, Peiping, forwarding Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese requisitioning of Chinese carts and nighttime movements of equipment northward.
subfiles.summary: Japanese military authorities reportedly requisitioned large numbers of Chinese carts in the Tongliao and Siping areas. Trains loaded with military equipment were also moving north through Mukden at night. The source believed these activities were related to the Russian situation.

subfiles.title: Telegram 181 on troop trains through Seoul
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, Tokyo, forwarding the Consul General at Seoul
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese troop trains passing through Seoul toward Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Troop trains passed through Seoul on November 16 and 18, with more expected on November 23 and 24. The movements were officially presented as replacements, but numbers were unknown and further inquiry was considered inadvisable.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for rumored troop movements from Japan to Manchuria
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch concerning unverified rumors of troop movements to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to despatch 247 and another file. It records rumors that troops were moving from Japan to Manchuria but identifies the information as unverified.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Japanese troop movements at Peiping and Shanhaiguan
subfiles.about: Indexes reports of arriving troops in Peiping and a southbound train from Shanhaiguan.
subfiles.summary: The note reports the arrival of Japanese infantry in Peiping. It also records that a Japanese troop train passed through Shanhaiguan from the north, with its destination unknown.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for northward movement through Mukden
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that Japanese troops were moving north through Mukden.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to telegram 73 and a related file. It describes a northward movement through Mukden by troops arriving from Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram 73 on a Japanese division moving north through Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports that a Japanese division from Japan was passing northward through Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Jellentine relayed reliable information that a Japanese division had moved north through Mukden during the preceding several days. A copy of the information was sent by mail to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for movement toward Outer Mongolia
subfiles.about: Indexes a report of troops and armament moving north from Mukden in possible preparation for action against Outer Mongolia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to telegram 84 and another file. It says Chinese observers interpreted the buildup as preparation for a movement against Outer Mongolia.

subfiles.title: Telegram 84 on northbound troop trains and armor at Mukden
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, Peiping, forwarding the Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports nightly troop trains and the loading of armored equipment at Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Two troop trains were reportedly being sent north each night while armored cars, tanks, and trucks were loaded at Mukden. Chinese circles believed a pretext would soon be arranged for a movement against Outer Mongolia. The report was repeated to Nanking and Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Letter on large troop embarkations at Kobe
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the embarkation of several thousand Japanese troops and supplies aboard transports at Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Eight transports were present on April 7–8, and McConaughy estimated that at least five thousand and possibly more than seven thousand troops embarked. Their uniforms suggested that they were recent conscripts probably destined for Manchuria, northern Korea, or the Shandong Peninsula to join the Kwantung Army or reinforce the Soviet frontier. The letter also notes troop movements toward Hiroshima, transports sailing west from Osaka, and temporary restrictions on commercial traffic in Kobe.

subfiles.title: Letter on troop embarkation at Hiroshima
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the embarkation of approximately three thousand troops at Hiroshima on April 13, 1938.
subfiles.summary: Dependable sources placed about three thousand troops aboard transports at Hiroshima. The letter states that the troops came from a unit stationed at Himeji. The document's own date is not legible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Kobe troop and casualty-ship movements
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on outward troop movements and returning ships carrying wounded men and soldiers' ashes.
subfiles.summary: The sheet associates the movements with the Sino-Japanese conflict. It records newly uniformed troops leaving Kobe by sea and vessels returning from China with wounded personnel and the ashes of the dead.

subfiles.title: Confidential distribution of Japanese Army divisions
subfiles.to: Military Aide to the President; Secretary of War; State Department; Secretary of the Treasury; Assistant Secretary of War; Chief of Staff; War Plans Division; Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Lists the reported geographic distribution of Japanese Army divisions in Japan, Korea, Manchuria, China, and Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum assigns numbered divisions to locations including Nanjing, the eastern Yangtze region, Canton, Korea, Hailar, northern Manchuria, Zhangjiakou, Suiyuan, Tianjin, Taiwan, Shandong, Hebei, Jiangxi, Hubei, Henan, Shanxi, and central China. Several readings are badly corrupted, and one eastern Yangtze formation is explicitly marked as of doubtful existence. The final page supplies the distribution list for senior military, naval, State, and Treasury officials.
